bull_thesis: Groupe SEB is Europe's dominant small-appliance group (Tefal, Krups, Moulinex, Rowenta, WMF, Supor) trading at a depressed price after a genuinely bad 2025 — and the bull case is that 2025 was a cyclical trough, not a structural break. bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a low-return, slow-melting franchise whose 'turnaround' is a three-year promise management itself won't underwrite. interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Groupe SEB (SK.PA)

*A deep dive on management and the setup. Groupe SEB is the French maker of small kitchen and home appliances — Tefal, Krups, Moulinex, Rowenta, WMF, Supor — split into a large Consumer division and a smaller, higher-margin Professional (commercial coffee and culinary equipment) division. Note: the transcript bundle is mixed and contains one stray call from SEB the Swedish bank (October 2024); that call is unrelated to this company and is ignored below. The analysis rests on the four genuine Groupe SEB calls: full-year 2024 (February 2025), Q1 2025 (April 2025), full-year 2025 (February 2026), and Q1 2026 (April 2026).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has shifted decisively over five quarters, from confident growth to a defensive turnaround.

In early 2025 (the full-year 2024 call), chief executive Stanislas de Gramont led with strength: a record EUR 8.27 billion in sales, operating profit up "over 10%," a 9.7% operating margin, and a dividend raised 6.9%. The frame was expansion — new acquisitions (Sofilac, La Brigade de Buyer in professional cookware), a new manufacturing hub in China, and a buoyant small-appliance market driven by innovation. Management spoke of consumer categories growing "9% outside of China."

By the Q1 2025 call (April 2025), the tone turned to weathering a storm. The headline was tariffs: the U.S. had just imposed steep duties, and most of the call was spent reassuring analysts that cookware fell under the milder Section 232 steel/aluminum regime (45% total) rather than the 145% reciprocal tariff, and that production could be relocated from China to Vietnam "by the end of this year or early part of next year." De Gramont conceded "the year will be shaky."

The full-year 2025 call (February 2026) was the inflection. Sales were essentially flat (+0.3% organic), operating profit (ORfA, "operating result from activity") fell EUR 201 million to EUR 601 million, and the operating margin collapsed from 9.7% to 7.4%. Management blamed "significant cyclical headwinds on currencies, on Americas, on Professional" worth roughly EUR 120 million. The big new element: the "Rebound plan," a EUR 200 million recurring cost-savings program with up to 2,100 job cuts (500 in France), explicitly designed "to bring the group back to a profitable growth trajectory." The growth story was quietly demoted; the new story is self-help margin repair.

By Q1 2026 (April 2026), the narrative is "early proof the plan is working": ORfA up 42% year on year to EUR 72 million and margin up 1.2 points to 3.8% — though management was candid that this was "supported by a favorable base effect because the Q1 ORfA of last year was low by historic standards."

The arc, in one line: a confident innovation-led grower in early 2025 became a margin-defending restructurer by 2026, with the entire investment case now hinging on a multi-year cost plan rather than on top-line momentum.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Sustained growth … small-appliance market remains resilient" | Revenue 2021 EUR 8.06B → 2025 EUR 8.17B; 3-yr revenue CAGR +0.9%, latest year −1.2% | Poorer than the story. The top line is flat-to-declining, not "sustained growth." |
| "We confirmed operating profit growth … 9.7% margin" (FY24) | True for 2024, but net income fell to EUR 232M (from EUR 386M in 2023) and EPS to EUR 4.23 (from EUR 6.97) | The operating headline masked a sharp fall in bottom-line earnings — partly the EUR 190M French competition fine, but the trend was already weak. |
| "Results are down in 2025 … margin 7.4%" | Confirmed: ORfA EUR 601M (−EUR 201M); net income EUR 245M; EPS EUR 4.45 | Honest. Management did not dress up a bad year. |
| "Strong cash discipline … normative free cash flow" | Free cash flow margin just 0.3%; FCF down ~94% year on year; price-to-FCF a distorted 105x | Far poorer than the narrative. Cash generation effectively evaporated in the latest year — the single ugliest number in the file. |
| "Net financial debt EUR 2.34 billion, leverage stable at ~1.8x EBITDA" | Confirmed; net debt recomputed at EUR 2.34B (EUR 2.15B ex-fine). Altman-Z 2.9 (grey zone) | Accurate, and leverage is manageable, not alarming. |
| "Return to growth in China" | China did return to ~3.5% organic growth in Q1 2025 and held through 2025 | Holds up — a genuine green flag. |
| EPS trajectory | 2021 EUR 8.36 → 2025 EUR 4.45; 5-yr EPS CAGR −14.6% | The most damning long-run number: earnings per share have roughly halved in four years. |

The pattern: management is honest about the bad year (a credibility positive), but the multi-year financials are materially weaker than the "resilient grower" framing — earnings per share have fallen by half since 2021, and free cash flow has collapsed.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: **Declining**, then stabilizing into cautious defense.

- FY2024 call (Feb 2025) — offensive and confident: "a very rich year … sustained growth … we will weather these uncertainties and convert growth into profit growth."
- Q1 2025 (Apr 2025) — defensive, hedged: "facing stormy conditions … the year will be shaky … it's very early to say, and we're certainly not ready to commit." A clear pivot from growth language to macro-survival language.
- FY2025 (Feb 2026) — contrite but determined: "2025 has been a rather difficult year … we are creating the conditions to see 2025 as an inflection point." Heavy emphasis on cost, savings, and "financial discipline" rather than growth.
- Q1 2026 (Apr 2026) — guarded optimism: "a solid quarter … on track … the context is getting more and more uncertain and deteriorated, yet we are on track." Confidence is returning but tethered tightly to the cost plan, not the market.

The vocabulary shift is the tell: from "innovation," "growth drivers," and "expansion" in early 2025 to "margin protection," "cost savings," "structural cost base," and "Rebound" by 2026.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Reliability: **Medium.**

The encouraging signal is that management revised guidance down in October 2025 and then *met the revised targets* — "we are in line with the targets that we revised in October." That is the behavior of a team that re-baselines honestly rather than serially missing. The screener also records a 100% beat rate (1 of 1 quarters), and consensus forward EPS growth of +46% off the depressed base.

The concern is that the team has not yet demonstrated it can deliver the *new* promise. The 10% (then 11%) operating-margin ambition is a 2028 target — three years out — and the bulk of the EUR 200 million savings lands in 2027, with management explicitly cautioning "it's too early to be very precise on the timing." A multi-year self-help target from a company whose margin just fell from 9.7% to 7.4% has to be scored Medium until execution shows through. The Q1 2026 margin jump is real but flattered by an easy comparison, as management itself volunteered — a point in their favor for candor, against the headline.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Tariffs and China sourcing** dominated 2025: analysts (HSBC, Equita) pressed repeatedly on U.S. exposure and the cost of relocating production. Management's answers were reassuring and, so far, broadly borne out — the Section 232 change proved "almost neutral," and Q1 2026 even flagged a tariff-reimbursement claim as a potential one-off positive.
- **The Rebound plan's timing and reinvestment** was the recurring 2026 question (Kepler Cheuvreux pressed twice): how much of the EUR 200 million lands in 2026, and how much gets reinvested. Management was vague — "a small portion" in 2026, "most … in 2027," and notably refused to commit the savings to flow through to margin, saying investment and savings are "two separate things." That refusal is the soft spot: it lets the savings be absorbed by reinvestment rather than dropping to the bottom line.
- **Sales growth versus margin** (Kepler again): analysts worry the 10% margin needs sales growth the company isn't delivering. De Gramont's answer was telling — he wants to "desensitize" the financial targets from the organic-growth ambition, i.e. hit margin via cost even if growth stays soft. That is a tacit admission that top-line recovery is not assured.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Red flags**
- Earnings per share roughly halved from EUR 8.36 (2021) to EUR 4.45 (2025); 5-year EPS CAGR −14.6%.
- Free cash flow collapsed ~94% year on year to a 0.3% FCF margin — a distorted 105x price-to-FCF.
- Operating margin fell from 9.7% to 7.4% in a single year.
- Return on invested capital just 6.4% — below a reasonable cost of capital, meaning the business is barely earning its keep at current returns.
- The whole investment case now rests on a three-year cost plan whose benefits management won't commit to dropping to margin.

🟢 **Green flags**
- Management re-based guidance honestly in October 2025 and then met it — a credibility marker.
- China returned to growth and the Consumer division held positive like-for-like through 2025 and into Q1 2026 (+2.9%).
- Strong innovation cadence with real revenue: washer-vacuums hit ~EUR 100M in year one, garment steamers ~EUR 90M, spot cleaners ~EUR 25M.
- Leverage is contained (~1.8x EBITDA; Altman-Z 2.9), so there is no balance-sheet emergency forcing a fire sale.
- Piotroski score 8/9 (a high mark on accounting quality and fundamental trend), and a dividend held flat rather than cut — the yield base is intact.
- Q1 2026 ORfA +42% and margin +1.2 points — the first datapoint that the plan and base effects are turning profitability up.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The clearest hidden signal is De Gramont's wish to "desensitize" financial targets from organic growth. Translated: management has lost confidence that the small-appliance market will reliably grow 5% a year, so they are re-engineering the model to deliver returns on cost discipline alone. That is a strategic concession dressed as discipline.
- The refusal to ring-fence the EUR 200 million savings for margin (vs. reinvestment) means the headline savings number may overstate the eventual margin lift.
- Germany is a persistent sore spot named in every recent call ("an underperformance in Germany that we need to deal with") — a structural, not cyclical, weakness in a core European market.
- The professional coffee business is increasingly the strategic darling (new China hub, new Peak/Elevation machines, Luckin Coffee as the biggest customer), but it is small (~12% of sales) and lumpy on large-contract phasing — it cannot carry the group.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **PIVOTING.** Groupe SEB is mid-turn — from an innovation-led grower to a cost-disciplined margin-repair story. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a self-help restructuring with no hard, binding catalyst and a payoff that is mostly 2027–2028; the value case rests on whether a EUR 200 million cost plan actually lands in margin (which management pointedly would not promise) against a flat-to-declining top line and a return on capital below its cost.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and currently ERODING.** The moat type is intangible brand (Tefal, Krups, Moulinex, WMF, Supor) plus scale in distribution and manufacturing. These are real, durable brands with genuine pricing/innovation ability — but the returns evidence says the moat is not protecting earnings right now: return on invested capital is just 6.4%, return on equity 10.4%, the operating margin fell from 9.7% to 7.4%, and free cash flow collapsed. A franchise earning below its cost of capital with falling margins is, by the evidence, an eroding moat regardless of brand strength.

**Secular threat: manageable.** Small kitchen appliances are not facing a structural, terminal demand killer — there is no streaming-style disruption or AI-displacement here. The pressures are cyclical and operational: currency, tariffs, Chinese demand softness, raw-material inflation, and a weak German market. The category itself ("consumers consistently keep equipping themselves with more small domestic equipment") is intact. The cheapness is therefore best read as a cyclical/operational fear-print on a low-return year, not a value trap over a melting base — provided the cost plan and free-cash-flow normalization actually arrive.

# Forensic Dossier — Groupe SEB (SK.PA)

*A deep dive on management and the setup. Groupe SEB is the French maker of small kitchen and home appliances — Tefal, Krups, Moulinex, Rowenta, WMF, Supor — split into a large Consumer division and a smaller, higher-margin Professional (commercial coffee and culinary equipment) division. Note: the transcript bundle is mixed and contains one stray call from SEB the Swedish bank (October 2024); that call is unrelated to this company and is ignored below. The analysis rests on the four genuine Groupe SEB calls: full-year 2024 (February 2025), Q1 2025 (April 2025), full-year 2025 (February 2026), and Q1 2026 (April 2026).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has shifted decisively over five quarters, from confident growth to a defensive turnaround.

In early 2025 (the full-year 2024 call), chief executive Stanislas de Gramont led with strength: a record EUR 8.27 billion in sales, operating profit up "over 10%," a 9.7% operating margin, and a dividend raised 6.9%. The frame was expansion — new acquisitions (Sofilac, La Brigade de Buyer in professional cookware), a new manufacturing hub in China, and a buoyant small-appliance market driven by innovation. Management spoke of consumer categories growing "9% outside of China."

By the Q1 2025 call (April 2025), the tone turned to weathering a storm. The headline was tariffs: the U.S. had just imposed steep duties, and most of the call was spent reassuring analysts that cookware fell under the milder Section 232 steel/aluminum regime (45% total) rather than the 145% reciprocal tariff, and that production could be relocated from China to Vietnam "by the end of this year or early part of next year." De Gramont conceded "the year will be shaky."

The full-year 2025 call (February 2026) was the inflection. Sales were essentially flat (+0.3% organic), operating profit (ORfA, "operating result from activity") fell EUR 201 million to EUR 601 million, and the operating margin collapsed from 9.7% to 7.4%. Management blamed "significant cyclical headwinds on currencies, on Americas, on Professional" worth roughly EUR 120 million. The big new element: the "Rebound plan," a EUR 200 million recurring cost-savings program with up to 2,100 job cuts (500 in France), explicitly designed "to bring the group back to a profitable growth trajectory." The growth story was quietly demoted; the new story is self-help margin repair.

By Q1 2026 (April 2026), the narrative is "early proof the plan is working": ORfA up 42% year on year to EUR 72 million and margin up 1.2 points to 3.8% — though management was candid that this was "supported by a favorable base effect because the Q1 ORfA of last year was low by historic standards."

The arc, in one line: a confident innovation-led grower in early 2025 became a margin-defending restructurer by 2026, with the entire investment case now hinging on a multi-year cost plan rather than on top-line momentum.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Sustained growth … small-appliance market remains resilient" | Revenue 2021 EUR 8.06B → 2025 EUR 8.17B; 3-yr revenue CAGR +0.9%, latest year −1.2% | Poorer than the story. The top line is flat-to-declining, not "sustained growth." |
| "We confirmed operating profit growth … 9.7% margin" (FY24) | True for 2024, but net income fell to EUR 232M (from EUR 386M in 2023) and EPS to EUR 4.23 (from EUR 6.97) | The operating headline masked a sharp fall in bottom-line earnings — partly the EUR 190M French competition fine, but the trend was already weak. |
| "Results are down in 2025 … margin 7.4%" | Confirmed: ORfA EUR 601M (−EUR 201M); net income EUR 245M; EPS EUR 4.45 | Honest. Management did not dress up a bad year. |
| "Strong cash discipline … normative free cash flow" | Free cash flow margin just 0.3%; FCF down ~94% year on year; price-to-FCF a distorted 105x | Far poorer than the narrative. Cash generation effectively evaporated in the latest year — the single ugliest number in the file. |
| "Net financial debt EUR 2.34 billion, leverage stable at ~1.8x EBITDA" | Confirmed; net debt recomputed at EUR 2.34B (EUR 2.15B ex-fine). Altman-Z 2.9 (grey zone) | Accurate, and leverage is manageable, not alarming. |
| "Return to growth in China" | China did return to ~3.5% organic growth in Q1 2025 and held through 2025 | Holds up — a genuine green flag. |
| EPS trajectory | 2021 EUR 8.36 → 2025 EUR 4.45; 5-yr EPS CAGR −14.6% | The most damning long-run number: earnings per share have roughly halved in four years. |

The pattern: management is honest about the bad year (a credibility positive), but the multi-year financials are materially weaker than the "resilient grower" framing — earnings per share have fallen by half since 2021, and free cash flow has collapsed.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: **Declining**, then stabilizing into cautious defense.

- FY2024 call (Feb 2025) — offensive and confident: "a very rich year … sustained growth … we will weather these uncertainties and convert growth into profit growth."
- Q1 2025 (Apr 2025) — defensive, hedged: "facing stormy conditions … the year will be shaky … it's very early to say, and we're certainly not ready to commit." A clear pivot from growth language to macro-survival language.
- FY2025 (Feb 2026) — contrite but determined: "2025 has been a rather difficult year … we are creating the conditions to see 2025 as an inflection point." Heavy emphasis on cost, savings, and "financial discipline" rather than growth.
- Q1 2026 (Apr 2026) — guarded optimism: "a solid quarter … on track … the context is getting more and more uncertain and deteriorated, yet we are on track." Confidence is returning but tethered tightly to the cost plan, not the market.

The vocabulary shift is the tell: from "innovation," "growth drivers," and "expansion" in early 2025 to "margin protection," "cost savings," "structural cost base," and "Rebound" by 2026.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Reliability: **Medium.**

The encouraging signal is that management revised guidance down in October 2025 and then *met the revised targets* — "we are in line with the targets that we revised in October." That is the behavior of a team that re-baselines honestly rather than serially missing. The screener also records a 100% beat rate (1 of 1 quarters), and consensus forward EPS growth of +46% off the depressed base.

The concern is that the team has not yet demonstrated it can deliver the *new* promise. The 10% (then 11%) operating-margin ambition is a 2028 target — three years out — and the bulk of the EUR 200 million savings lands in 2027, with management explicitly cautioning "it's too early to be very precise on the timing." A multi-year self-help target from a company whose margin just fell from 9.7% to 7.4% has to be scored Medium until execution shows through. The Q1 2026 margin jump is real but flattered by an easy comparison, as management itself volunteered — a point in their favor for candor, against the headline.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Tariffs and China sourcing** dominated 2025: analysts (HSBC, Equita) pressed repeatedly on U.S. exposure and the cost of relocating production. Management's answers were reassuring and, so far, broadly borne out — the Section 232 change proved "almost neutral," and Q1 2026 even flagged a tariff-reimbursement claim as a potential one-off positive.
- **The Rebound plan's timing and reinvestment** was the recurring 2026 question (Kepler Cheuvreux pressed twice): how much of the EUR 200 million lands in 2026, and how much gets reinvested. Management was vague — "a small portion" in 2026, "most … in 2027," and notably refused to commit the savings to flow through to margin, saying investment and savings are "two separate things." That refusal is the soft spot: it lets the savings be absorbed by reinvestment rather than dropping to the bottom line.
- **Sales growth versus margin** (Kepler again): analysts worry the 10% margin needs sales growth the company isn't delivering. De Gramont's answer was telling — he wants to "desensitize" the financial targets from the organic-growth ambition, i.e. hit margin via cost even if growth stays soft. That is a tacit admission that top-line recovery is not assured.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Red flags**
- Earnings per share roughly halved from EUR 8.36 (2021) to EUR 4.45 (2025); 5-year EPS CAGR −14.6%.
- Free cash flow collapsed ~94% year on year to a 0.3% FCF margin — a distorted 105x price-to-FCF.
- Operating margin fell from 9.7% to 7.4% in a single year.
- Return on invested capital just 6.4% — below a reasonable cost of capital, meaning the business is barely earning its keep at current returns.
- The whole investment case now rests on a three-year cost plan whose benefits management won't commit to dropping to margin.

🟢 **Green flags**
- Management re-based guidance honestly in October 2025 and then met it — a credibility marker.
- China returned to growth and the Consumer division held positive like-for-like through 2025 and into Q1 2026 (+2.9%).
- Strong innovation cadence with real revenue: washer-vacuums hit ~EUR 100M in year one, garment steamers ~EUR 90M, spot cleaners ~EUR 25M.
- Leverage is contained (~1.8x EBITDA; Altman-Z 2.9), so there is no balance-sheet emergency forcing a fire sale.
- Piotroski score 8/9 (a high mark on accounting quality and fundamental trend), and a dividend held flat rather than cut — the yield base is intact.
- Q1 2026 ORfA +42% and margin +1.2 points — the first datapoint that the plan and base effects are turning profitability up.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The clearest hidden signal is De Gramont's wish to "desensitize" financial targets from organic growth. Translated: management has lost confidence that the small-appliance market will reliably grow 5% a year, so they are re-engineering the model to deliver returns on cost discipline alone. That is a strategic concession dressed as discipline.
- The refusal to ring-fence the EUR 200 million savings for margin (vs. reinvestment) means the headline savings number may overstate the eventual margin lift.
- Germany is a persistent sore spot named in every recent call ("an underperformance in Germany that we need to deal with") — a structural, not cyclical, weakness in a core European market.
- The professional coffee business is increasingly the strategic darling (new China hub, new Peak/Elevation machines, Luckin Coffee as the biggest customer), but it is small (~12% of sales) and lumpy on large-contract phasing — it cannot carry the group.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **PIVOTING.** Groupe SEB is mid-turn — from an innovation-led grower to a cost-disciplined margin-repair story. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a self-help restructuring with no hard, binding catalyst and a payoff that is mostly 2027–2028; the value case rests on whether a EUR 200 million cost plan actually lands in margin (which management pointedly would not promise) against a flat-to-declining top line and a return on capital below its cost.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and currently ERODING.** The moat type is intangible brand (Tefal, Krups, Moulinex, WMF, Supor) plus scale in distribution and manufacturing. These are real, durable brands with genuine pricing/innovation ability — but the returns evidence says the moat is not protecting earnings right now: return on invested capital is just 6.4%, return on equity 10.4%, the operating margin fell from 9.7% to 7.4%, and free cash flow collapsed. A franchise earning below its cost of capital with falling margins is, by the evidence, an eroding moat regardless of brand strength.

**Secular threat: manageable.** Small kitchen appliances are not facing a structural, terminal demand killer — there is no streaming-style disruption or AI-displacement here. The pressures are cyclical and operational: currency, tariffs, Chinese demand softness, raw-material inflation, and a weak German market. The category itself ("consumers consistently keep equipping themselves with more small domestic equipment") is intact. The cheapness is therefore best read as a cyclical/operational fear-print on a low-return year, not a value trap over a melting base — provided the cost plan and free-cash-flow normalization actually arrive.

By Q1 2026 (April 2026), the narrative is "early proof the plan is working": ORfA up 42% year on year to EUR 72 million and margin up 1.2 points to 3.8% — though management was candid that this was "supported by a favorable base effect because the Q1 ORfA of last year was low by historic standards."

The arc, in one line: a confident innovation-led grower in early 2025 became a margin-defending restructurer by 2026, with the entire investment case now hinging on a multi-year cost plan rather than on top-line momentum.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Sustained growth … small-appliance market remains resilient" | Revenue 2021 EUR 8.06B → 2025 EUR 8.17B; 3-yr revenue CAGR +0.9%, latest year −1.2% | Poorer than the story. The top line is flat-to-declining, not "sustained growth." |
| "We confirmed operating profit growth … 9.7% margin" (FY24) | True for 2024, but net income fell to EUR 232M (from EUR 386M in 2023) and EPS to EUR 4.23 (from EUR 6.97) | The operating headline masked a sharp fall in bottom-line earnings — partly the EUR 190M French competition fine, but the trend was already weak. |
| "Results are down in 2025 … margin 7.4%" | Confirmed: ORfA EUR 601M (−EUR 201M); net income EUR 245M; EPS EUR 4.45 | Honest. Management did not dress up a bad year. |
| "Strong cash discipline … normative free cash flow" | Free cash flow margin just 0.3%; FCF down ~94% year on year; price-to-FCF a distorted 105x | Far poorer than the narrative. Cash generation effectively evaporated in the latest year — the single ugliest number in the file. |
| "Net financial debt EUR 2.34 billion, leverage stable at ~1.8x EBITDA" | Confirmed; net debt recomputed at EUR 2.34B (EUR 2.15B ex-fine). Altman-Z 2.9 (grey zone) | Accurate, and leverage is manageable, not alarming. |
| "Return to growth in China" | China did return to ~3.5% organic growth in Q1 2025 and held through 2025 | Holds up — a genuine green flag. |
| EPS trajectory | 2021 EUR 8.36 → 2025 EUR 4.45; 5-yr EPS CAGR −14.6% | The most damning long-run number: earnings per share have roughly halved in four years. |

The pattern: management is honest about the bad year (a credibility positive), but the multi-year financials are materially weaker than the "resilient grower" framing — earnings per share have fallen by half since 2021, and free cash flow has collapsed.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: **Declining**, then stabilizing into cautious defense.

- FY2024 call (Feb 2025) — offensive and confident: "a very rich year … sustained growth … we will weather these uncertainties and convert growth into profit growth."
- Q1 2025 (Apr 2025) — defensive, hedged: "facing stormy conditions … the year will be shaky … it's very early to say, and we're certainly not ready to commit." A clear pivot from growth language to macro-survival language.
- FY2025 (Feb 2026) — contrite but determined: "2025 has been a rather difficult year … we are creating the conditions to see 2025 as an inflection point." Heavy emphasis on cost, savings, and "financial discipline" rather than growth.
- Q1 2026 (Apr 2026) — guarded optimism: "a solid quarter … on track … the context is getting more and more uncertain and deteriorated, yet we are on track." Confidence is returning but tethered tightly to the cost plan, not the market.

The vocabulary shift is the tell: from "innovation," "growth drivers," and "expansion" in early 2025 to "margin protection," "cost savings," "structural cost base," and "Rebound" by 2026.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Reliability: **Medium.**

The encouraging signal is that management revised guidance down in October 2025 and then *met the revised targets* — "we are in line with the targets that we revised in October." That is the behavior of a team that re-baselines honestly rather than serially missing. The screener also records a 100% beat rate (1 of 1 quarters), and consensus forward EPS growth of +46% off the depressed base.

The concern is that the team has not yet demonstrated it can deliver the *new* promise. The 10% (then 11%) operating-margin ambition is a 2028 target — three years out — and the bulk of the EUR 200 million savings lands in 2027, with management explicitly cautioning "it's too early to be very precise on the timing." A multi-year self-help target from a company whose margin just fell from 9.7% to 7.4% has to be scored Medium until execution shows through. The Q1 2026 margin jump is real but flattered by an easy comparison, as management itself volunteered — a point in their favor for candor, against the headline.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Tariffs and China sourcing** dominated 2025: analysts (HSBC, Equita) pressed repeatedly on U.S. exposure and the cost of relocating production. Management's answers were reassuring and, so far, broadly borne out — the Section 232 change proved "almost neutral," and Q1 2026 even flagged a tariff-reimbursement claim as a potential one-off positive.
- **The Rebound plan's timing and reinvestment** was the recurring 2026 question (Kepler Cheuvreux pressed twice): how much of the EUR 200 million lands in 2026, and how much gets reinvested. Management was vague — "a small portion" in 2026, "most … in 2027," and notably refused to commit the savings to flow through to margin, saying investment and savings are "two separate things." That refusal is the soft spot: it lets the savings be absorbed by reinvestment rather than dropping to the bottom line.
- **Sales growth versus margin** (Kepler again): analysts worry the 10% margin needs sales growth the company isn't delivering. De Gramont's answer was telling — he wants to "desensitize" the financial targets from the organic-growth ambition, i.e. hit margin via cost even if growth stays soft. That is a tacit admission that top-line recovery is not assured.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Red flags**
- Earnings per share roughly halved from EUR 8.36 (2021) to EUR 4.45 (2025); 5-year EPS CAGR −14.6%.
- Free cash flow collapsed ~94% year on year to a 0.3% FCF margin — a distorted 105x price-to-FCF.
- Operating margin fell from 9.7% to 7.4% in a single year.
- Return on invested capital just 6.4% — below a reasonable cost of capital, meaning the business is barely earning its keep at current returns.
- The whole investment case now rests on a three-year cost plan whose benefits management won't commit to dropping to margin.

🟢 **Green flags**
- Management re-based guidance honestly in October 2025 and then met it — a credibility marker.
- China returned to growth and the Consumer division held positive like-for-like through 2025 and into Q1 2026 (+2.9%).
- Strong innovation cadence with real revenue: washer-vacuums hit ~EUR 100M in year one, garment steamers ~EUR 90M, spot cleaners ~EUR 25M.
- Leverage is contained (~1.8x EBITDA; Altman-Z 2.9), so there is no balance-sheet emergency forcing a fire sale.
- Piotroski score 8/9 (a high mark on accounting quality and fundamental trend), and a dividend held flat rather than cut — the yield base is intact.
- Q1 2026 ORfA +42% and margin +1.2 points — the first datapoint that the plan and base effects are turning profitability up.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The clearest hidden signal is De Gramont's wish to "desensitize" financial targets from organic growth. Translated: management has lost confidence that the small-appliance market will reliably grow 5% a year, so they are re-engineering the model to deliver returns on cost discipline alone. That is a strategic concession dressed as discipline.
- The refusal to ring-fence the EUR 200 million savings for margin (vs. reinvestment) means the headline savings number may overstate the eventual margin lift.
- Germany is a persistent sore spot named in every recent call ("an underperformance in Germany that we need to deal with") — a structural, not cyclical, weakness in a core European market.
- The professional coffee business is increasingly the strategic darling (new China hub, new Peak/Elevation machines, Luckin Coffee as the biggest customer), but it is small (~12% of sales) and lumpy on large-contract phasing — it cannot carry the group.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **PIVOTING.** Groupe SEB is mid-turn — from an innovation-led grower to a cost-disciplined margin-repair story. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a self-help restructuring with no hard, binding catalyst and a payoff that is mostly 2027–2028; the value case rests on whether a EUR 200 million cost plan actually lands in margin (which management pointedly would not promise) against a flat-to-declining top line and a return on capital below its cost.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and currently ERODING.** The moat type is intangible brand (Tefal, Krups, Moulinex, WMF, Supor) plus scale in distribution and manufacturing. These are real, durable brands with genuine pricing/innovation ability — but the returns evidence says the moat is not protecting earnings right now: return on invested capital is just 6.4%, return on equity 10.4%, the operating margin fell from 9.7% to 7.4%, and free cash flow collapsed. A franchise earning below its cost of capital with falling margins is, by the evidence, an eroding moat regardless of brand strength.

**Secular threat: manageable.** Small kitchen appliances are not facing a structural, terminal demand killer — there is no streaming-style disruption or AI-displacement here. The pressures are cyclical and operational: currency, tariffs, Chinese demand softness, raw-material inflation, and a weak German market. The category itself ("consumers consistently keep equipping themselves with more small domestic equipment") is intact. The cheapness is therefore best read as a cyclical/operational fear-print on a low-return year, not a value trap over a melting base — provided the cost plan and free-cash-flow normalization actually arrive.
